Hannah Wilson · Applied AI

A household scheduler that reasons about hand-offs

Every week, one person in a household holds the whole plan in their head: who is home when, who covers the gap between the au pair leaving and a parent getting back, who cooks, when a sitter needs booking. This turns three Google Calendars, a notes graph and a household database into one message the family and the caregiver can both act on — and, more usefully, flags the places where the week does not actually work.

Open the live demo → Real UI, fictional household, no sign-in.

The problem it solves

A shared calendar tells you what is scheduled. It does not tell you that Thursday is broken. The information needed to notice that is spread across four places that never meet: the work calendar knows a meeting runs to 6:30, the household database knows the au pair's contract ends at 6:30, a config value knows the commute is 35 minutes, and nothing at all knows that the other parent is away that night. The gap only becomes visible when you join all four — which is exactly the joining a person does in their head every Sunday evening.

The output is deliberately a message, not a dashboard. It has to be pasteable into a family chat and readable by a caregiver on a phone, which is why the artifact is plain text with emoji rather than a UI nobody outside the household will log into.

A generated week ends with the part that actually earns its keep — the asks, derived rather than transcribed:

‼️ Flags & asks: • Thu: 40min coverage gap — Inês ends 6:30, Priya home ~7:10, Dan away. @Inês can you stay until 7:15? That's 45min overtime 🐣 • Sat: sitter needed 6:45pm–late, both parents out. Book by Wednesday 🐣 • Inês is at 27.5h before Friday — Friday needs 2.5h to hit the 30h target

None of those three lines appears on any calendar. Each is the result of joining a meeting end-time to a commute estimate to a contracted finish time to a weekly hours target.

Three decisions worth defending

Conflict detection lives in the prompt, not in Python

The obvious build is a rules engine: intervals per person, detect overlaps, emit conflicts. I started there and abandoned it. The rules that matter are not interval overlaps — they are "a two-year-old cannot be left with a six-year-old", "45 minutes before the event if both parents are out", "the commute makes a 6:30 finish a 7:10 arrival". Encoding those as predicates produced a combinatorial mess that broke on every household change, and the household changes constantly.

Stating them as constraints in the system prompt and letting the model do the joining collapsed several hundred lines of brittle logic and — the part I did not expect — handled cases I never enumerated, like noticing that a 6:10 arrival for a 6:30 family dinner has no slack in it.

The trade-off: non-determinism in something a family relies on. Mitigated by keeping the output honest rather than confident — every inference is phrased as an ask a human confirms, and a deterministic post-pass scrapes the warning markers back out into structured flags, so a missed warning is visible as an empty chip row rather than silent.

The unstructured output gets structured on the way back out

Claude returns a WhatsApp message. The UI needs badges, history and search. Rather than force the model into JSON — which degraded the prose quality that is the entire point of the artifact — the app generates prose and then re-derives structure from it: _extract_flags() scrapes lines carrying warning markers or keywords like coverage gap and overtime, dedupes them, and surfaces them as chips.

The trade-off: a heuristic over generated text is not a contract. It is cheap and it degrades gracefully — a missed line costs a chip, not a broken response — which is the right failure mode for a badge. It would be the wrong one for anything downstream depends on.

Everything a life change touches is editable in the UI

The first version kept the household in YAML. It stopped being used the week a job changed, because updating it meant editing a file. Now people, pets, contracted caregiver hours, work days, commute times and the dinner rota are all editable from the Configuration page and written back to Supabase; the app-behaviour settings that stay in YAML are round-tripped with ruamel so a save does not strip the file's comments.

People edits reconcile rather than append — a row you delete is deleted, with foreign keys cascading or nulling — because the alternative is a config file that only ever grows.

The trade-off: a schema to migrate instead of a file to edit. Worth it: the tool is only useful if it survives contact with a household that changes.

Stack

LayerChoice
GenerationAnthropic API — system prompt per output format, household constraints in the user prompt
DataSupabase / Postgres — household, contracted hours, recurring events, run history
CalendarsGoogle Calendar API, OAuth, three calendars merged and regex-filtered
NotesOpen Brain (OB1) knowledge graph over MCP — free-text capture, entity extraction
ServerFastAPI — a JSON API of ~14 endpoints
Front endOne HTML file, vanilla JS, no build step
This demoThe same front end, with a shim answering /api/* from fixtures

What the demo is and is not

  • Is: the production front end, unmodified, built from the same template file the running app renders. The Configuration, Calendar and History views are fully interactive.
  • Is not: a live generation. Run schedule replays a schedule the real pipeline produced for the fictional week rather than calling Claude — a static site cannot hold an API key, and one that could would be a key anyone could spend.
  • Fictional throughout. The household, the employer, the calendars and the generated week are invented for this page. No real family data is published here.
